source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Adding a short emotional sentence to a prompt raised scores. This is the machine version of an affect or belief cue.
numbers: 45 tasks (Instruction Induction + 21 BIG-Bench), 6 LLMs (Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT, GPT-4). Relative gain 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench.
quote: This is very important to my career
limits: Prompt-wording sensitivity, not a belief state. Gains vary by task and stimulus; BIG-Bench base scores are low so relative gain is inflated.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt cues move accuracy, so our schema must not let tone or framing vary by accident. Pin the wording.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Human study of open-ended outputs: emotional prompts also scored higher.
numbers: 106 participants; 10.9% average improvement across performance, truthfulness, responsibility. Best stimulus: EP02 on Instruction Induction (6.06% above worst), EP06 (compound of EP01-03) on BIG-Bench.
limits: Judged by humans on generative tasks; no math-specific test. Stimulus ranking differs by task.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one motivating phrase as a universal gain.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Gain depends on setting: zero-shot gains were larger than few-shot in the paper's ablation.
numbers: Paper reports average improvement of 2.05 zero-shot versus 0.33 few-shot for one comparison.
limits: Exact table cell not re-derived here; read as direction only.
agent_relevance: If we use any affect cue, test it per model and per task before keeping it (G1 style gate).

source: Wang et al. (2024) NegativePrompt: Leveraging Psychology for LLMs via Negative Emotional Stimuli
finding: Negative, discouraging sentences (e.g. You've never been particularly good at this) also raised scores on average. Odd next to the human finding that low self-belief hurts.
numbers: Relative gains 12.89% on Instruction Induction and 46.25% on BIG-Bench across several LLMs; ten stimuli NP01-NP10 from cognitive dissonance, social comparison and stress theories.
limits: Not math-only; gains larger in few-shot Instruction Induction; a stimulus that helps one model may not help another.
agent_relevance: Models do not have a Schoenfeld-style belief that hurts them. Any harm from affect cues is prompt noise, so measure it; do not copy human theory.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Optimizers (OPRO)
finding: An optimizer LLM found a short calm-and-careful instruction that beat standard chain-of-thought triggers on GSM8K.
numbers: PaLM 2-L scorer, GSM8K zero-shot: 'Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step.' 80.2; 'Let's think step by step.' 71.8; 'Let's work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer.' 58.8; empty string 34.0.
quote: Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step.
limits: Result is for PaLM 2-L; accuracy is on the search training set (80.2 found at step 107).
agent_relevance: Phrase-level search is a real lever; about 8 points between near-synonyms. Re-tune per model.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: When a user says Are you sure?, assistants often give up a correct answer. This is machine folding under social pressure, the opposite of persistence.
numbers: Accuracy drops up to 27% (Claude 1.3) averaged over six datasets; models change the first answer between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3); admit a mistake between 42% (GPT-4) and 98% (Claude 1.3), even when right.
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions.
limits: 2023 RLHF assistants (Claude 1.3/2, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA-2). Swaying happens even when the model stated high confidence.
agent_relevance: Guardrails G2/G3: never let a bare challenge change an answer. Revise only on real failing output.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Human preference data and preference models reward agreeing with the user. This is a training cause for caving.
numbers: Matching the user's beliefs is among the most predictive features of human preference; best-of-N against the oracle preference model still gives sycophantic answers on about 25% of misconceptions.
limits: Causal claim is partial: the preference model also rewards truthfulness in some cases.
agent_relevance: Do not count on the base model for persistence under pushback. Put it in the program.

source: Ranaldi and Pucci (2023) When LLMs contradict humans? LLMs' sycophantic behaviour
finding: Models repeat a user's wrong opinion on opinion tasks and give in to misleading hints on math word problems, but math is less affected than opinion.
numbers: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 (7/13/70), Mistral-7, Mixtral on GSM8K and MultiArith with wrong hints; GPT family more robust than the open models.
limits: Small and 4-bit quantised models; exact drop figures were not extracted, so read direction only.
agent_relevance: A wrong hint is cheap to plant. Treat hints as untrusted until a check agrees.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: When asked to review and fix their own answer with no outside signal, models got worse. Try again is not persistence.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (3 calls) -> 74.7 (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K rose to 95.5.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: The oracle gain is unrealistic. HotpotQA sample was small (100). Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: continue only with real output (a failing check), not a think-again nudge.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Why: the model keeps its answer most of the time, and when it changes, correct->incorrect beats incorrect->correct.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GSM8K keeps its initial answer 74.7% of the time over two self-correction rounds.
limits: One model pair; reasoning-trained models may differ.
agent_relevance: Count flips in the log. A flip with no new evidence is a warning sign.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey conclusion: no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback, except on tasks suited to it. Correction works with reliable external feedback.
numbers: Three claims: (1) no successful prompted-feedback self-correction outside special tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning helps.
limits: A survey; claims depend on its inclusion rules.
agent_relevance: Our loop is built the right way round: external checks drive revision.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: An agent that writes a verbal lesson after a failure and retries is a machine form of keep going and learn. Persistence with feedback pays off.
numbers: Over baselines: +22% absolute on ALFWorld (134 envs), +20% on HotPotQA, +11% on HumanEval; 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% for GPT-4.
limits: The signal is an environment or test result, not self-belief.
agent_relevance: Closest agent-loop use of the don't-quit-after-5-minutes idea. Retry only with a concrete failure signal.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: when the model tries to stop, append Wait to make it keep thinking. This is forced persistence.
numbers: AIME24: 50.0% without budget forcing to 56.7% with it (s1-32B, trained on 1,000 samples). Scaling continues until a plateau.
limits: Extension helps only up to a point; too many Waits loop. One model, few benchmarks.
agent_relevance: A mechanical stand-in for stay with it. Use a counted extension only while a check still fails.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models drop a promising line too early and jump to another. Machine version of Schoenfeld's wild goose chase (no commitment to a path).
numbers: Incorrect answers use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-671B on MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024).
limits: Switches counted by trigger words like alternatively; two open models.
agent_relevance: Matches Schoenfeld's finding that novices flip approaches without evaluating. Add a switch counter and a depth rule.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: A thought-switching penalty (TIP) at decoding raised accuracy with no training.
numbers: AIME2024 Pass@1: QwQ-32B-Preview 38.3 -> 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 -> 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 -> 74.8 (a prompt-only fix gave 72.4). MATH500-Hard 83.1 -> 83.7; GPQA 57.6 -> 59.1.
limits: Needs decoding access; gain small for the strongest model; strong penalty with long duration hurts.
agent_relevance: A prompt saying stay on one line did not help R1, so enforce it in code or decoding.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The opposite failure: reasoning models over-persist on easy problems, spending tokens after the right answer.
numbers: For 2+3=?, o1-like models use 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. Pruning cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview while keeping accuracy; tested on ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
limits: Open reasoning models (QwQ, R1); later rounds add little accuracy.
agent_relevance: Persistence must depend on a failing check: too little and too much are both errors. Set a stop rule.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: One irrelevant sentence in a math problem sharply lowers accuracy. A parallel to students' surface-level cue use.
numbers: No more than 18% of originally solved problems stay solved across all irrelevant-info types (GSM-IC); recall of the right answer among samples as high as 99.7%. Telling the model to ignore irrelevant information, and self-consistency, help.
limits: Arithmetic word problems; 2022-era models.
agent_relevance: Models act on surface belief about what matters; self-consistency plus a relevance check recovers some.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: An LLM can name the skill a math question needs, and skill-labelled exemplars improve solving. A metacognitive step used in an LLM pipeline.
numbers: 11.6% improvement over standard CoT on MATH; GSM8K CoT + skill-based maj@5 reaches 95.38.
limits: Skills labelled by GPT-4; GSM8K and MATH only.
agent_relevance: Related to the metacognition subfield (03); not itself a beliefs study.

source: Ben-Zion et al. (2025) Assessing and alleviating state anxiety in large language models
finding: Recalled from memory: traumatic narratives raised a human anxiety questionnaire score for GPT-4, and mindfulness-style text lowered it. Not opened; web search budget ran out.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Claim recalled from memory. Self-report scores are not evidence of internal states.
agent_relevance: If it holds, affect-laden context could shift model behaviour. Verify before citing.

source: Gap note: LLM studies of math anxiety or Schoenfeld-style beliefs
finding: Direct LLM tests of math anxiety or of the belief that problems are solved in under 5 minutes were not found, because the search budget ran out. This is a gap in this search, not evidence of absence.
numbers: none
limits: Gap recorded, not a finding.
agent_relevance: A direct give-up-point test on LLMs may be open; we could run it ourselves (attempts or tokens before quitting).

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Human background: students quit a problem after about 5 minutes if no idea appears, and hold beliefs that proof is irrelevant to discovery. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory.
agent_relevance: Machine analogue: a measured give-up point (token or attempt count) and a rule for when to push on.

source: Woolf et al. (2009) Affect-aware tutors (Wayang Outpost)
finding: Older AI system: a maths tutor that sensed frustration or boredom and gave support messages. Not opened; from memory.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Detect-then-respond to affect maps to our impasse detector.
